source_text: Ioviniano autem in una parte coniungeris; nam dicit in secundo operis sui libro, baptizatum hominem non posse peccare; ante Baptisma autem et peccare et non peccare posse. Tecum ergo putat, a tempore Baptismatis imponi hominibus necessitatem boni; quod aeque falsum est, quam quod tu putas, ante Baptisma inesse hominibus necessitatem faciendi mali. Nam cum dicis tu: Non potest homo boni aliquid velle, nisi adiuvetur ab eo, qui malum non potest velle [n257] ; participatione utique gratiae et naturae bonae vis hominem possibilitatem consequi faciendi boni; quod dicis tamen a tempore Baptismatis posse contingere. Inter impietatem igitur medius et timorem, ad Ioviniani consortium confugisti, sed Manichaei lupanar necdum reliquisti. Verumtamen tanto te innocentior Iovinianus, quanto Ioviniano profanior Manichaeus. Ut enim adhuc brevius quod egimus colligatur, Manichaeus dicit: In omnibus hominibus inspiratrix malae voluntatis tenebrarum natura delinquit, et aliud facere non potest. Tu dicis: In cunctis hominibus primi peccati tenebris infecta, et per hoc malae voluntatis auctor natura delinquit, et bonum velle non potest. Iovinianus dicit: Voluntas quidem hominum, sed usque ad Baptisma delinquit; postea autem nisi bonum velle non potest. Catholici, id est nos, dicimus, quod ab initio usque ad finem sine aliquo naturalium coactu, voluntas et ante Baptisma in unoquoque delinquit, quae illo ipso tempore quo peccat, potestatem habet recedere a malo, et facere bonum, ut constet ratio libertatis. Vestrum itaque nulli quidem veritas dogmatum constat; tamen cum ab uno principio erroris fueritis egressi, vel minus inhonestum erat, si quae consequuntur admitteres, et quia cum Manichaeo dicis, natura mala, id est, manca libertate delinqui, diceres cum eodem, nullo illam pacto posse mundari; quod quidem alibi affirmas; sed quod necessario consequebatur, adiungeres ideo ei opus non esse baptismatis sacramentis. Aut si cum Ioviniano, a tempore susceptae fidei imprimi asseris bonas cupiditates; diceres cum eodem, bonam et ante Baptisma fuisse naturam, quae licet haberet possibilitatem mali, non tamen habuerit necessitatem, ac per hoc ad indissimulabile bonum consecrata pervenerit. Hoc enim modo, etsi rationi, nequaquam tamen eorum, quos sequeris, dogmatibus contravenires.
pass_a_gloss: But to Jovinian you are joined in one part; for he says in the second book of his work, that a baptized human cannot sin; but before Baptism he can both sin and not sin. With you therefore he thinks, that from the time of Baptism a necessity of good is imposed on humans; which is equally false as what you think, that before Baptism there is in humans a necessity of doing evil. For when you say: A human cannot will anything of good, unless he is helped by him, who cannot will evil; by participation at any rate of grace and of a good nature you want a human to obtain the possibility of doing good; which you say nevertheless can happen from the time of Baptism. Between impiety therefore and fear in the middle, you have fled to the consortium of Jovinian, but you have not yet left the brothel of the Manichaean. Nevertheless Jovinian is so much more innocent than you, as the Manichaean is more profane than Jovinian. That what we have driven may still be gathered more briefly, the Manichaean says: In all humans the nature of darkness, inspirer of an evil will, offends, and cannot do another thing. You say: In all humans nature infected by the darknesses of the first sin, and through this author of an evil will, offends, and cannot will good. Jovinian says: The will indeed of humans, but up to Baptism offends; but afterward it cannot will unless good. Catholics, that is we, say, that from the beginning unto the end without any coaction of natural things, the will even before Baptism offends in each one, which at that very time at which it sins, has the power of receding from evil, and of doing good, that the account of liberty may stand. To none of you therefore does the truth of dogmas stand; nevertheless since you went out from one principle of error, it was even less dishonorable, if you would admit the things which follow, and because with the Manichaean you say, that it is offended by an evil nature, that is, with maimed liberty, you would say with the same, that it can by no pact be cleansed; which indeed elsewhere you affirm; but what was necessarily following, you would join that therefore there is no need for it of the sacraments of baptism. Or if with Jovinian, from the time of faith taken up you assert that good desires are impressed; you would say with the same, that nature was good even before Baptism, which although it had the possibility of evil, nevertheless did not have the necessity, and through this consecrated arrived at an undisguisable good. For in this manner, even if you would contravene reason, nevertheless by no means the dogmas of those whom you follow.

LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'

pass_b_english: You are joined to Jovinian on one point. In the second book of his work he says that a baptized person cannot sin, while before baptism a person can both sin and refrain from sin. With you, then, he thinks that from the time of baptism a necessity of good is imposed on human beings. This is just as false as your belief that before baptism human beings possess a necessity of doing evil. For when you say, “A human being cannot will anything good unless helped by the one who cannot will evil” (Augustine, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 1.7), you mean that through sharing in grace and a good nature a person obtains the capacity to do good; you say, however, that this can happen from the time of baptism. Caught between impiety and fear, you have therefore fled to Jovinian's company, but have not yet left Mani's brothel. Yet Jovinian is as much more innocent than you as Mani is more profane than Jovinian.

To gather up our argument still more briefly: the Manichaean says, “In all human beings the nature of darkness, which inspires the evil will, sins and cannot do anything else.” You say, “In all human beings nature, infected by the darkness of the first sin and therefore the author of an evil will, sins and cannot will good.” Jovinian says, “The human will does indeed sin, but only up to baptism; afterward it can will nothing but good.” Catholics, that is, we, say that from beginning to end there is no compulsion from anything belonging to nature. In each person it is the will that sins, including before baptism; at the very time it sins it has the power to depart from evil and do good, so that freedom remains a reality.

None of you therefore possesses true doctrine. Nevertheless, since you set out from a single starting point of error, it would at least have been less dishonorable to accept the consequences. Since you say with Mani that sin occurs through an evil nature, that is, through defective freedom, you should also have said with him that it cannot be cleansed in any way. You do affirm this elsewhere; but you should have added its necessary consequence, that it therefore has no need of baptism's sacraments. Or if you assert with Jovinian that good desires are imprinted from the time faith is received, you should have said with him that nature was good even before baptism: although it had the capacity for evil, it did not have its necessity, and so by consecration it reached an unmistakable good. In this way, even if you opposed reason, at least you would not contradict the doctrines of those you follow.

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
